stories.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
stories.summary: Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found. The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10. They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine. And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed. Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking. In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show. Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally. The review, external of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws. It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC. One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals. "Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body." The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.

stories.title: A nosy polar bear and a lucky squirrel: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 shortlist
stories.summary: How would it feel to find yourself face to face with one of the Arctic's most formidable predators? This stunning image captures life from a seal's perspective. Taken by Norwegian wildlife photographer Audun Rikardsen, it was among the 'Highly Commended' entries in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition. While working as a guide with Arctic Wildlife Tours, Rikardsen rigged an underwater camera with a motion sensor beneath a seal's breathing hole, and then waited. At 4am, a female polar bear approached and peered down. Rikardsen then waited eight hours for the bear to move away before retrieving the camera and reviewing the images. When he saw what he had captured, he said: "I was so extremely happy. I was screaming, so I probably woke up all the polar bears for miles." Rikardsen has previously won two Wildlife Photographer of the Year categories: Birds in 2019 and Oceans: The Bigger Picture in 2025. The overall winners will be announced on Tuesday 13 October 2026, followed by an exhibition at the Natural History Museum in London, external from Friday 16 October 2026. Scroll down to explore other highly commended works from the competition. Crockford watched swifts return to London after their annual migration from Africa, filling the air with their high-pitched calls.
